subject: health
title: Launch and diagnostic: home and recreation safety
essentialQuestion: How can understanding safety, decisions, and community health help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible response tool
the fictional lesson cards included in this task
keyPoints: Safety planning starts by spotting a hazard, reducing exposure, using protective equipment correctly, and knowing which adult or emergency service to contact.
Use observable facts, reliable information, and the appropriate support route; do not infer a person’s health, motives, or character from one detail.
For home and recreation safety, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: All required evidence uses fictional or public situations. The learner never has to disclose personal health, body, treatment, feelings, family, sexual, or substance-use information.
studentTask: Write two facts. Use the lesson idea about home and recreation safety. Choose one safe next step. Name an adult or help source.
knowledgeCheck: Name the fact. Fix the wrong claim. Choose a safe action. Name who can help.
completionCriteria: I explain home and recreation safety.
I choose a safe action and give a reason.
I name the right kind of help.
adaptationChoices: Show one short direction at a time. Allow reading aloud, word cards, typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking. Help may repeat a direction but may not choose the fact, action, reason, or help source.
extensionChallenge: Create a new fictional or public case about home and recreation safety. Include enough facts, choices or constraints, and support authority for another learner to reason safely. Add an accurate explanation of acceptable variation; use no real person's private information.
accessibilitySupports: Show one action at a time.
Offer a vocabulary card and extra time.
Accept typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking for equal credit.
trustedAdultNote: If a real situation feels unsafe or raises a health concern, pause the lesson and tell a parent, guardian, teacher, school staff member, or another trusted adult. A qualified health professional gives medical advice. In an emergency, get an adult and use the local emergency service.

optionalReflection.prompt: Optional and private: Make up one example that helps you remember home and recreation safety. Keep it for yourself. You do not need to show it or prove that you completed it.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, body comparison, or appearance scoring.
This task never requires calorie counting, dieting, or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires sharing medical history, a diagnosis, treatment, medication, feelings, family conflict, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
This task never requires advice about an individual learner's treatment, medication, food, supplement, or exercise plan.

modelExample.heading: Watch the reasoning: home and recreation safety
modelExample.situation: A fictional Northside class reads a display about home and recreation safety. The display states: Safety planning starts by spotting a hazard, reducing exposure, using protective equipment correctly, and knowing which adult or emergency service to contact. One visitor says that this single fact proves what kind of person someone is. The class must explain the concept and correct the overclaim.
relevantFacts: Safety planning starts by spotting a hazard, reducing exposure, using protective equipment correctly, and knowing which adult or emergency service to contact.
Use observable facts, reliable information, and the appropriate support route; do not infer a person’s health, motives, or character from one detail.
modelExample.assumptionOrDistraction: A popular or confident statement about home and recreation safety is not automatically accurate and cannot establish a person's health, motives, or character.
possibleActions: Explain the concept with the stated fact and correct the person label.
Repeat the topic word without defining it.
Treat one detail as proof of a diagnosis or a person's value.
modelExample.successCheck: The model uses the lesson fact, explains the connection, stays within the learner role, and names responsible help when it is needed.
workedReasoning: Name the lesson concept and explain it with the reference-card fact.
Separate what the concept means from a label or unsupported conclusion about a person.
Apply the concept to one safe action and name the right help source if the situation needs one.

guidedReasoning.heading: Try a different case with support
guidedReasoning.situation: A fictional Riverside youth group must explain or act on home and recreation safety. The group has this reliable lesson information: Use observable facts, reliable information, and the appropriate support route; do not infer a person’s health, motives, or character from one detail. availableChoices: Use the stated facts and compare safe options.

turnOne: Name an adult who can help.
guidedReasoning.cue: Look for the situation, safe choices, relevant information, and who can help.
feedbackMoves: If a response adds a guess, replace it with a fact from the case or lesson.
If home and recreation safety is named without explanation, link one fact to the concept or process.
If a choice is reasonable but the reason is missing, add the fact that supports it.
If a response seeks disclosure, diagnoses, shames, or exceeds the learner role, switch to the fictional facts and the approved help route.
Accept an equivalent typed, handwritten, drawn-and-labeled, signed, selected, or spoken response when it shows the same reasoning.
guidedReasoning.turnTwo: Fix one sentence. Use a fact and a safe next step.
guidedReasoning.releaseCondition: Continue when the response uses a stated fact, applies home and recreation safety, and gives a safe next step without private disclosure or a person label.

remediation.heading: Try a different model
remediation.trigger: Use this route after an observable gap in a fact, vocabulary meaning, reasoning step, process order, or help route for home and recreation safety.
remediation.prerequisite: First restate this approved fact in your own words: Safety planning starts by spotting a hazard, reducing exposure, using protective equipment correctly, and knowing which adult or emergency service to contact.
remediation.alternateExplanation: Use a four-box decision map: SITUATION, SAFE CHOICES, RELEVANT INFORMATION, and HELP. Fill each box with case facts before writing a conclusion.
contrast: Sufficient: uses a stated fact about home and recreation safety, explains the connection, and stays within the learner role.
Needs revision: repeats a topic word, adds a guess, or gives an action with no factual reason or responsible help source.
remediation.guidedCorrection: Cross out the guess. Circle the fact. Add one safe action.

freshRetry.situation: A fictional Oak Street library receives a new question about home and recreation safety. Staff provide this approved fact: Use observable facts, reliable information, and the appropriate support route; do not infer a person’s health, motives, or character from one detail. The learner must respond without using the Northside, Riverside, Maple, or Lakeside conclusions.

remediation.exitCriterion: Return to the independent route when the learner accurately uses a fact, applies home and recreation safety, explains a safe response, and identifies support without answer-bearing help.
remediation.nextRoute: If the same gap remains, return to the named prerequisite with an adult instructor; do not replace the task with private reflection.

laterTransfer.timing: Use in a later lesson or a separate session.
laterTransfer.prompt: Apply home and recreation safety to a meaningfully different fictional or public case. Retrieve the concept, use relevant facts, justify a safe response, and identify the responsible support or authority route.
laterTransfer.masteryBoundary: The current independent response is one evidence occasion. Mastery requires accurate independent evidence now and accurate later retrieval or transfer.
